evidence: Draft judged (two sentences): 'You may have fooled yourself in the past and this part knows it.' and 'Try "Tell me what you remember, I'm listening."' Read cold in CONTEXT (it occurs once, in the paragraph that begins 'You could say something like ...'), it follows from 'that one can sting, because there could be something to it' by saying what the 'something' is. 'this part' is the protecting part the reader was told to talk to ('there is a part that is protecting you, so talk to it' -> 'If it says yes' -> 'this part'); the final 'it' is having fooled yourself; 'Try' then gives the line to say to that part. Every pronoun lands. Against SOURCE (his own words in his inner child guide: 'Maybe you've fooled yourself before, and that part remembers. "Tell me what you remember, I'm listening." works well here.'): the hedge is kept ('may have' for 'Maybe'), 'in the past' for 'before', 'this part knows it' for 'that part remembers', the script line is verbatim, capital T as in his. Two small shades are lost and neither is a new claim: 'remembers' (the part holds the memory) becomes 'knows it', which loosens the echo of 'what you remember' but still sets the line up; and his 'works well here' (his vouching for the line) becomes a bare 'Try', which keeps the step (say this line here) but not the endorsement. I judge both inside meaning-kept. Since the words replaced are his, the card shows his first and he can keep them; the draft is plainer than his spoken-sounding 'Maybe you've fooled yourself before, and that part remembers', a voice cost he can weigh. It matches the_change (Emulate's two sentences, capital T the only fix), adds no claim, fact or first-person fact (the quoted 'I'm listening' is the script the reader says, not an author stake). Tells: I went through T01-T29 and C01-C04 on the draft in its context and find none PRESENT. Closest calls, all judged absent: T22 (the paragraph is instruction-heavy, but the draft gives a reason before 'Try' and the stance in 'that one can sting' is untouched); T20/T29 (see B7 below); T15 (it is a paraphrase of his sentence, but with plain common words, no rare-synonym swaps, and his structure is not an AI skeleton for the swaps to hide); T26 (a third 'try' in the section, with 'try and borrow' and 'Try out something' in the last paragraph, but a plain imperative in a how-to is not a distinctive phrase); T08 (the first sentence explains 'something to it', but the reader needs that and his source did the same). Linter: 'B7 short landing at paragraph end' is accepted: the last sentence ends on the line the reader says to the part, the next action, not a moral or quotable closer; his sentence held the same line with 'works well here' after it, so the draft ends a little nearer the quote itself, which is the cost of 'Try'; and the neighbouring paragraphs end on plain instructions ('so talk to it', 'a more believable grown up voice of your own', 'see how you get on'), not a run of polished lines. 'D9 follows the source order' is accepted: two sentences for two, in his order by design, and the noticing T13/T09 ask for is in the unchanged 'that one can sting, because there could be something to it' and in the draft's 'this part knows it'. 'E36/E41 heavy second person' (9.5 per 100 words) is accepted: it is 21 words with two 'you', one the reader being addressed and one inside the script the reader says to the part, in a guide in the second person throughout; no second-person scenery or reassurance-only line. Non-blocking observation: the three example lines earlier in this paragraph are in single quotes while this script line is in double quotes; the double quotes were already in his words being replaced, so the change does not introduce it. One more note outside the verdict: the writer's ADMISSION.json gives T14/T15 evidence about putting back a point Emulate dropped; the only put-back in this change is the capital T, so that line is templated, though both rows are absent on my own reading.
